results.key_finding: Non-contrast CT head is required before lumbar puncture when any of the following are present: age >60, immunocompromise, history of CNS disease, new-onset seizure, papilledema, abnormal level of consciousness, or focal neurological deficit. results.authors: Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D.
results.key_finding: S. pneumoniae accounts for approximately 50% of community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults and carries the highest case-fatality rate. Focal neurologic deficits including seizures predict a complicated course. Early identification of CT-before-LP indications prevents iatrogenic herniation. Lumbar puncture is safe when non-contrast CT shows no mass effect, midline shift, or basal cistern obliteration.
results.title: Community-Acquired Bacterial Meningitis in Adults

output.summary: IDSA 2004 guidelines specify that non-contrast CT head must precede lumbar puncture when age >60, new-onset seizure, altered level of consciousness, focal neurological deficit, papilledema, or immunocompromise are present. A clear CT (no mass effect, no shift, no herniation) permits immediate LP. Empiric antibiotics (vancomycin + third-generation cephalosporin; add ampicillin if Listeria risk) and dexamethasone must be initiated without delay — no more than 60 minutes from clinical suspicion — even before LP results are available. Blood cultures must precede the first antibiotic dose. Dexamethasone should be given before or concurrently with the first antibiotic dose; delayed administration provides no outcome benefit.

Do NOT withhold dexamethasone because LP is pending; dexamethasone must precede or accompany the first antibiotic dose — even before the LP is performed.

key_clinical_evidence: The combination of age >60, new-onset focal seizure, altered mental status, AND a focal neurological deficit (right pronator drift and extensor plantar response) satisfies four simultaneous IDSA 2004 criteria for CT-before-LP: all four must be recognized together to correctly sequence the workup.

A clear CT (no mass effect, no shift, no herniation, patent basal cisterns) permits immediate lumbar puncture — a normal CT does NOT by itself diagnose or exclude meningitis, but it confirms LP is mechanically safe.

Empiric antibiotics and dexamethasone must NOT be delayed for the CT or LP: the 60-minute window from clinical suspicion begins at triage, not at CT or CSF results. Blood cultures before antibiotics is mandatory; LP should precede antibiotics if obtainable within 30 minutes, but must not cause delay beyond 60 minutes.

The focal right-sided seizure and motor deficit create a powerful stroke-anchoring trap: a naive workup focused on stroke would delay CT-head-to-LP-to-antibiotics sequencing and miss empiric treatment of a time-critical CNS infection.

Neutrophilic pleocytosis with critically low CSF glucose ratio (0.17), markedly elevated protein (284 mg/dL), Gram-positive diplococci, and positive pneumococcal antigen are individually each confirmatory of bacterial meningitis; their combination is definitive.

Inhaled corticosteroid use in COPD is not equivalent to systemic immunosuppression and does not independently mandate CT before LP, but the patient's four other criteria each independently mandate it.

Adjunctive dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg IV q6h x 4 days) before or with the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and unfavorable outcomes specifically in pneumococcal meningitis; administration after antibiotics provides no benefit.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Patricia Holt is a 64-year-old right-handed White woman with a history of COPD on inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting beta-agonist therapy, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia who is brought to the emergency department by EMS after a witnessed focal seizure at home. Per her neighbor who called 911, Ms. Holt had been complaining of severe bifrontal headache and neck pain since yesterday morning, and appeared increasingly confused and disoriented throughout the day. She reportedly told her neighbor she "couldn't think straight" and was "burning up." This evening, the neighbor witnessed Ms. Holt suddenly develop rightward head turning and right arm tonic posturing lasting approximately 90 seconds, followed by secondary generalization with bilateral convulsions, which terminated spontaneously. The neighbor denied any prior history of seizures, head trauma, or similar episodes. EMS found Ms. Holt post-ictally confused with a temperature of 38.8 degrees Celsius, heart rate of 114, blood pressure of 152/88, and oxygen saturation of 91% on room air. She was administered supplemental oxygen en route. She did not receive any anticonvulsants prehospital.

On arrival in the ED, Ms. Holt remains markedly confused and disoriented. She is unable to provide meaningful history. Review of her medication bottles confirms current use of inhaled fluticasone/salmeterol and tiotropium for COPD, amlodipine, and rosuvastatin. She has never received pneumococcal vaccination. There is no family member present. The neighbor reports no recent antibiotic use, no sick contacts, no recent travel, and no prior neurological conditions. She denies known immunodeficiency, but her COPD is managed with inhaled corticosteroids.

On examination she has marked nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, severe photophobia, a subtle right facial droop, right pronator drift, and an extensor plantar response on the right. These focal signs in the setting of age >60, AMS, and a recent seizure mandate non-contrast CT head BEFORE lumbar puncture per IDSA 2004 guidelines.
